name: Cordyceps sinensis (Ophiocordyceps)

lead: Ophiocordyceps sinensis, formerly Cordyceps sinensis, is a fungus that grows on ghost-moth larvae on the Tibetan Plateau. It is prized in traditional medicine and sold today as capsules and powders marketed for energy, stamina and recovery.

For appearance the chain is indirect: supporters take it to train harder and recover faster, which can mean more training volume and a better physique. Human trials on exercise performance have mixed results, with small randomized trials reporting both no change and positive changes in muscle and altitude-related measures.

paras: People use capsules or extracts of cultivated mycelium or the related Cordyceps militaris, often alongside other adaptogens such as rhodiola or in pre-workout blends, for weeks at a time. Marketing materials emphasize stamina and recovery.

Wild fruiting bodies often contain high arsenic and other metals, and China has regulated their sale since 2016. A review of supplements and bleeding loosely associated Cordyceps with surgical bleeding. Quality and species identification vary between products.

chain: Supplement taken for energy and stamina
angle.text: Users take cordyceps to support training output and recovery so they can train more, which over time feeds muscle and conditioning. It is also sold in wellness blends aimed at overall vitality.

lead: Ophiocordyceps sinensis, long called Cordyceps sinensis, is an insect-pathogenic fungus of the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas that infects ghost-moth larvae; its fruiting body, nicknamed the caterpillar fungus, is harvested for traditional medicine.[1] It appears in a late-15th-century Tibetan text as an aphrodisiac and in Wang Ang's 1694 Chinese materia medica.[1]

In looksmaxxing and fitness circles it is taken as a supplement intended to support endurance, energy and recovery, with the idea that more and better training leads to a fuller physique and leaner body. Products are commonly cultivated mycelium or the related Cordyceps militaris rather than wild caterpillar fungus.[1]

Human research is small and varied. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in amateur cyclists, a commercial blend with Cordyceps sinensis and rhodiola showed no significant effect on peak VO2, time to exhaustion or peak power.[2] A 2024 randomized trial examined pre-exercise Cordyceps supplementation and stem-cell recruitment to skeletal muscle after high-intensity interval exercise.[3]
infobox: Cordyceps sinensis; described 1843, moved to Ophiocordyceps in 2007 [1]
Up to about US$50,000 per pound [1]

paras: The fungus infects underground ghost-moth larvae and sends a fruiting body out of the soil. It is harvested in Tibet, Nepal and neighbouring regions and is a major cash source for rural households.[1]

Miles Berkeley described it in 1843 as Sphaeria sinensis, Saccardo moved it to Cordyceps in 1878, and molecular work placed it in Ophiocordyceps in 2007.[1] Prices rose about 900 percent from 1998 to 2008, and top grades reached about US$50,000 per pound in 2012.[1]

A 2008 report of cordycepin in the fungus used unverified material; a 2017 study found O. sinensis does not produce cordycepin. Cordycepin was originally discovered in Cordyceps militaris, a species cultivated in China, Vietnam, Taiwan and Indonesia and used as a substitute.[1] Fruiting bodies were first grown in a lab in 1983; mycelia are grown in liquid or on grain for supplements.[1]

A randomized crossover-style placebo-controlled trial in 17 amateur cyclists using a commercial Cordyceps and rhodiola blend reported no significant treatment effect on peak oxygen uptake, time to exhaustion or power output.[2] A 2024 randomized, double-blind trial studied Cordyceps supplementation and stem-cell recruitment in muscle after intense exercise.[3] A controlled trial of a rhodiola and Cordyceps supplement during short-term high-altitude training reported improved aerobic exercise performance.[4] Trials in Chinese renal-transplant and COPD patients also exist.[5]

Wild fruiting bodies often contain high arsenic and other heavy metals, which can make them toxic, and China regulated their sale in 2016.[1] A 2022 review of supplements and bleeding loosely associated Cordyceps sinensis with surgical bleeding independent of anticoagulants.[6]
